analysis.one_liner: Lets states set up their own universal health care systems using existing federal health dollars.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on July 25, 2024 with three Democratic sponsors and never received a hearing or vote, dying in the Senate Finance Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let any state apply to set up its own universal, publicly administered health coverage system. The state would get the federal money that would have gone to Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA subsidies, federal employee and military coverage for its residents, adjusted for caseload growth and inflation, and use it to run a plan covering everyone. Any state could have opted in, but the bill died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that adopt a plan would gain guaranteed comprehensive coverage regardless of job, income, or health status, with cost-sharing protections and a requirement to cover reproductive and gender-affirming care. States would gain control of a large pool of federal health dollars (including what would have been premium tax credits) plus any savings from administration, which they could reinvest in care. Uninsured people and people who fall through gaps between employer plans, Medicaid, and the exchanges would benefit most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: A state could apply for a waiver of the ACA, Medicaid, Medicare, CHIP, FEHB, TRICARE, and employer-mandate rules in order to run one comprehensive, publicly administered plan covering all of its residents.

Federal money that would otherwise have been spent on those programs for the state's residents would be passed through to the state — including premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies, adjusted for caseload growth and health inflation — and any savings would be available for reinvestment in health services.

The state plan must cover all residents with benefits at least as comprehensive and affordable as what they would have received under the federal programs, and must include reproductive health care, including abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care.

The bill builds in accountability: public notice and comment, an independent assessment panel that reviews every application, annual reports to Congress, and a five-year review with a requirement that the state reach 95 percent coverage or face waiver termination after a grace period.

analysis.who_pays: The plan must be budget-neutral for the federal government over a 10-year plan, so the federal government would pass through what it would have spent rather than pay more. The cost of covering everyone would fall on the state, which would need to raise financing from its own taxpayers; employers could also face new state financing arrangements. People satisfied with their current Medicare, TRICARE, FEHB, or private coverage in a participating state would be moved into the state plan.

drawbacks.text: Because the federal pass-through must be budget-neutral, a state would have to finance everything beyond that amount itself, meaning higher state taxes or spending to cover people who are uninsured or underinsured today.

A waiver sweeps in Medicare, TRICARE, FEHB, and employer coverage for the state's residents, so people who like their current federal or employer coverage would be moved into a new state-run system, with the transition risk that entails.

If a state misses the 95 percent coverage target, it gets technical assistance and a 12-month grace period, but the waiver can then be terminated — potentially disrupting coverage for everyone enrolled.
The mechanism only works state by state: residents of states whose governments choose not to apply get nothing, so the same bill produces universal coverage in some places and no change in others.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is unusually detailed with real guardrails — a federal budget-neutrality requirement, a 95 percent coverage target, public comment, an independent panel, and five-year reviews with termination power. The honest cost is that universal coverage must be paid for by the state, the transition would uproot coverage that many people are satisfied with, and the benefits only reach states willing and able to take it on. It was a genuine option for states, not a mandate — but it also died without ever being seriously examined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never gave it a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the State-Based Universal Health Care Act of 2024 on July 25, 2024, with Senators Warren and Merkley as cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare, Medicaid, and tax policy.
No further action was ever taken: the bill sat in the Finance Committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health coverage system — private insurers, employers, and the current federal programs — was untouched because no state was ever given the option to leave it. No senator ever had to vote on it publicly.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let states create universal health care systems using existing federal health dollars.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only senators to support it.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 25, 2024 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no partisan split can be measured; all three sponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill.

industries.note: In any state that adopted a waiver, the individual and much of the group insurance market would be replaced by a publicly administered state plan, and the state must raise awareness of restrictions on selling duplicative or supplemental private insurance. Insurers would lose premium revenue in waiver states, though states could still contract with private entities to administer the plan.

The bill lets a state waive the employer mandate and ERISA preemption, so employers could stop buying coverage for workers in a waiver state — but they could face new state financing for the universal system instead.
Providers would get paid by a single state payer at rates the state sets, and would benefit from treating fewer uninsured patients, but would lose the ability to negotiate with multiple payers.
